segments.text: By now, you likely know that AI converts text into tokens, and assigns each one a unique
numerical identifier called a token ID.
But there is a catch.
That number tells us absolutely nothing about what the word actually means.
Think of a high school cafeteria.
An ID identifies you.
It doesn't describe you.
If four students are wearing badges numbered 1024, 2048, 3072, and 4096, those numbers tell
us who is who.
But they tell us nothing about who is funny, who plays hockey, or who just stole French
fries off their friend's tray.
So how can numbers actually represent meaning?
Let's use a taste test analogy.
Imagine rating drinks on a scale from 0 to 10, where a higher number means a drink has
more of a certain trait.
This table shows how we will structure the test.
We have rows for the drinks, and we will judge them across six distinct characteristics.
Sweet, bitter, fizz, heat, caffeine, and dark.
By moving away from a single arbitrary ID number and building a grid of specific scores, we can
start mapping out complex real world traits.
You and your friends tasted coffee and rated it on six characteristics.
Let's put those ratings in the table.
Coffee scores one for sweet, nine for bitter, zero for fizz, nine for heat, eight for caffeine,
and ten for dark.
Next, you taste coke, and rate it on the same six characteristics.
Coke scores nine for sweet, one for bitter, ten for fizz, two for heat, three for caffeine,
and eight for dark.
Which drinks scores nine for sweet, one for bitter, and ten for fizz?
That is coke.
A row of numbers like this is called a vector.
Each position is a dimension, and the number there is its value.
By organizing these specific values across multiple dimensions, we generate a unique,
readable numerical fingerprint for the item we are describing.
Now let's add a third drink, Pepsi.
Look closely at the resulting data.
Pepsi's six values match coke's exactly.
If we hid the drink names, these numbers alone could not tell the two coals apart.
To solve this problem, let us introduce a new column.
Citrus gives us a seventh dimension.
When we rate the drinks for citrus flavor, coffee gets a zero,
coke gets a one, and Pepsi gets a ten.
The first six values still match, but their new seven number profiles are distinctly different.
Another dimension can capture a difference the earlier numbers missed.
AI uses this exact same numerical approach to represent the meaning of words.
That row is called an embedding.
This comparison table maps our taste test directly to an AI model.
In your test, every drink gets a row.
In AI, every single token in the model's vocabulary gets its own row.
For dimensions, your test used six, then seven.
To avoid the coke and Pepsi overlap issue across an entire language,
AI typically uses thousands of dimensions.
While you chose values on a zero to ten scale,
AI learns its values during training,
utilizing positive numbers, negative numbers, and decimals.
Your taste test captured named traits, like sweet and fizz.
AI captures complex, abstract patterns in how a token is actually used.
And while you provided human labels for the columns, an AI model has none.
The values simply work together to represent meaning.
Both use a row of numbers to describe something.
This diagram shows the embedding table inside an actual model.
When you type cat, the AI follows its token ID, 4719,
to find its matching row alongside all the other tokens.
The table starts with the token ID and the token itself,
followed by columns representing dimensions, marked D1 through Dn.
Reading across the row for cat, the first position is 0.45.
Then it drops to negative 0.23 and stretches across the
thousands of precise numerical positions.
A single learned number in this grid, like that 0.45,
is called a value or a parameter.
The complete continuous row of numbers is the embedding.
Even word fragments get their own embeddings.
A long word, like unbelievable, splits into three separate token rows,
each containing its own sequence of learned numbers.
AI uses numbers to work with meaning.
Those numbers help AI recognize similarities and differences.
